claims.text: The hybrid CE-ML-thermodynamic-integration framework will predict HEA melting temperatures with less than 5% error relative to experiment.
The framework will predict HEA entropies of fusion with less than 5% error relative to experiment.
The proposed framework will outperform standard CALPHAD extrapolations at extreme temperatures.
Refractory HEAs typically melt above 1500 K.
Short-range-order clusters and local lattice distortions significantly alter the vibrational density of states.
Short-range-order clusters and local lattice distortions significantly alter the free-energy barrier for melting.
Standard CALPHAD models rely on extrapolated binary and ternary parameters for multicomponent HEAs.
Such CALPHAD extrapolations fail to capture nonlinear interactions and strong local chemical ordering in HEAs.
An ML potential trained on DFT data can accurately model the anharmonic phonon spectrum of the HEA.
The ML potential can accurately model the configurational entropy of the liquid phase.
The configurational entropy of the liquid is often overestimated by harmonic approximations.
Cluster expansion enables efficient sampling of the HEA configurational space.
The ML potential provides high-energy liquid-state accuracy at lower computational cost than ab initio molecular dynamics over the entire phase space.
Entropy of fusion will increase with compositional complexity.
Enhanced vibrational anharmonicity is the cause of the predicted increase in entropy of fusion with compositional complexity.
Standard CALPHAD will deviate by more than 15% from experimental melting temperatures in the proposed regime.
Standard CALPHAD will fail to capture the nonlinear dependence of melting temperature on composition.
The method is valid for substitutional solid-solution HEAs whose liquid phase remains disordered.
The method may fail when strong intermetallic-compound formation dominates the phase diagram or when important liquid short-range order is absent from the ML training set.
Training only on configurations representative of 0 K or 300 K can introduce errors when the potential is applied in the high-temperature anharmonic regime.
